notes: Desk rule: a cost of the year whose bill is still to come (or came after 31 March) is credited to Expenses payable, never to the supplier’s own ledger. The one exception: a charge a platform keeps back from its payout is credited to that platform’s own ledger, as every payout is booked.
Prepaid and accrued amounts go by whole months.
New ledgers made for this close: Expenses payable (Current Liabilities), Prepaid insurance (Current Assets) and Depreciation (Indirect Expenses).
Work in rupees. I round the final statements to ₹ lakh.

tasks.title: Reconcile the bank at 31 March
tasks.prompt: Tick the bank book against the March statement, line by line; the April statement shows what cleared later. Put what is left under the four heads, 0 where a head is empty, then work out the bank balance the books should carry. Your BRS goes to Snehal when you move on.

lockOnLeave.note: You can’t change it after this.
lockOnLeave.done: Handed to Snehal. You can read your BRS but not change it.

hints: Tick by amount, not by date: a card settlement reaches the bank the day after the sale, and a cheque when the payee banks it.
Only what the bank did on its own (charges it took, money it received directly) is missing from the books. Cheques and deposits still on their way are not.
tasks.note: Type each head as a positive figure; its label says whether it is added or taken off. When the four heads are right, the book’s ₹6,92,300 lands exactly on the statement’s ₹7,75,320.

cells.line: Add: cheques issued, not yet presented

amt.working: Cheque 000418, Ashok Sathaye, 30 March: paid by the bank on 5 April

cells.line: Add: credited by the bank, not yet in the bank book

amt.working: Meter deposit refund from Indrayani Power, credited 29 March

cells.line: Less: receipts in the bank book, not yet credited by the bank

amt.working: Card and UPI sales of 31 March, credited on 1 April

cells.line: Less: debited by the bank, not yet in the bank book

amt.working: POS terminal rent for March, debited 31 March

cells.line: Bank balance the books should carry, once the bank’s own entries are in

notes.r1.amt: The Koregaon Park rent, net of TDS. Cheque 000417 to Mallandur was written a day earlier but cleared on the 31st, so it ticks.
notes.r2.amt: The old roastery meter’s deposit. The bank has it; the bank book doesn’t yet.
notes.r3.amt: Each day’s card money reaches the bank the next day, and for 31 March that day fell in April. The other days all tick.
notes.r4.amt: The bank’s monthly rent for the card machine. Nobody told the books.
notes.r5.amt: Only the bank’s two entries go into the books. The cheque and the card money are on their way, so ₹7,03,120 is the figure for the balance sheet, not the statement’s ₹7,75,320.

tasks.title: Pass the close entries
tasks.prompt: Ten items from Snehal’s close list, each with its papers. Where the books need an entry, pick the account to debit, the account to credit and the amount; where they don’t, say so. Your entries go to Snehal when you move on.

lockOnLeave.note: You can’t change them after this.
lockOnLeave.done: Handed to Snehal. You can read your entries but not change them.

hints: For each paper ask two things: does the cost or the money belong to 2026–27, and is it already in the trial balance?
A suspense receipt is cleared to the ledger it should have gone to. Find whose money it was before you pick the credit.

fields.label: Amount
fields.invalidNote: Type the amount in rupees, like 1,25,000

fields.label: Narration, or why no entry
fields.placeholder: For example: being March telephone bill, payable in April

items.label: Suspense · NEFT of 18 March
items.note: NEFT of 18 March: Nilima Apte returned the deposit on the old Koregaon Park shop when Kaapi Kala moved out. Their own money coming back, not income. Suspense Dr, Security deposits Cr, ₹1,00,000.

items.label: Suspense · NEFT of 22 March
items.note: NEFT of 22 March: Pashan Cowork Hub paid invoice 0311, and their mail says so. The sale went into the books in February, so this only settles the debtor. Suspense Dr, Sundry debtors Cr, ₹1,24,000, and their ledger goes to nil.

items.label: Bank’s debit · POS terminal rent
items.note: POS rent: ₹1,180 for the card machine, taken by Satpura on 31 March. Bank charges Dr, Satpura Bank Cr, dated that day, not the day the books found it.

items.label: Bank’s credit · Meter deposit refund
items.note: Meter refund: the old roastery meter’s ₹12,000 deposit came back on 29 March. It sits in Security deposits, so that is the credit; Satpura Bank Dr. Calling it income would leave a deposit they no longer have and a profit they never made.

items.label: March power bills
items.note: Power bills: March’s units are March’s cost, whatever date the bill carries. ₹52,600 + ₹21,300 + ₹18,500 = ₹92,400. Electricity Dr, Expenses payable Cr, as the desk rule says.

items.label: March salaries
items.note: Salaries: no entry. JV 0218 already provided ₹3,96,000 on 31 March, and Salary payable shows it in the TB. The April batch only paid that liability. Varun’s entry would have counted March twice.

items.label: Shop and stock policy
items.note: Insurance: the policy runs 1 October to 30 September, and the desk counts whole months: six of its twelve belong to 2027–28. So ₹72,000, half the premium, goes to Prepaid insurance; Insurance Cr.

items.label: Depreciation 2026–27
items.note: Depreciation: none in the TB at all. The schedule gives ₹6,24,000 on equipment and ₹1,15,000 on the van: Depreciation Dr ₹7,39,000, credited to the two accumulated depreciation ledgers.

items.label: Cheque 000418
items.note: Cheque 000418: no entry. Ashok Sathaye banked it and it was paid on 5 April. A cheque on its way is a timing item. Reversing it would undo March rent they really paid.

items.label: FeastFleet orders of 30 and 31 March
items.note: FeastFleet: the ₹45,000 of orders is already in March sales and their ledger; booking ₹38,600 as April sales would count those orders twice. What is missing is the ₹6,400 commission: Commission Dr, FeastFleet (Sundry debtors) Cr, not Expenses payable, as they keep it back.

tasks.title: Tally the trial balance
tasks.prompt: Snehal has posted the reviewed close entries in Tally; the journal register is in Documents. On her TB summary, work out each changed group’s balance after the close, then the two totals. If the totals differ, a posting has gone the wrong way.

lockOnLeave.ask: Hand your TB summary to Snehal?
lockOnLeave.note: You can’t change it after this.
lockOnLeave.done: Handed to Snehal. You can read your TB summary but not change it.

hints: Post each entry to its ledger’s group: an asset or an expense rises with a debit, a liability or an income with a credit.
An entry between two ledgers of the same group (the bank and the deposits are both Current Assets) leaves that group’s total where it was.
tasks.note: Debit groups first, then credit groups. Each total adds its side’s groups after the close.

cells.g: Debit groups the close leaves alone: opening inventory, purchases
Credit groups the close leaves alone: capital, loans, sales

notes.cl.post: Only the March power bills touch this group: ₹92,400 into Expenses payable. Salaries were already here.
notes.fa.post: Depreciation is credited to the two accumulated depreciation ledgers, which sit inside Fixed Assets, so the group falls by ₹7,39,000.
notes.ca.post: The meter refund moves ₹12,000 from deposits to the bank, both in this group, so only the other five postings move the group.
notes.ie.post: Four postings add to expenses and one takes ₹72,000 out: the insurance that belongs to next year.
notes.sus.post: Nil. A suspense balance at the year-end means somebody’s money is still unexplained, and auditors ask about it first.
notes.tdr.post: Both sides fall by ₹1,31,600: the ₹2,24,000 of suspense goes and ₹92,400 of power bills comes in. Depreciation only moves value from Fixed Assets to expenses, both on the debit side.
notes.tcr.post: Equal to the debit side, so the TB tallies. It tallied before the close too, which is why a tally alone proves so little.

tasks.title: Draft the Schedule III figures
tasks.prompt: Map the trial balance after the close to Schedule III (Division I), in rupees; Snehal rounds the final set. The loan schedule, creditors list and stock papers are in Documents. The audit fee and Kunal’s tax figure come later, so stop at profit before tax.
hints: Principal that falls due by 31 March 2028 leaves long-term borrowings and joins short-term borrowings.
A manufacturer shows materials consumed and the change in finished goods, not purchases: opening plus purchases less closing, class by class.
tasks.note: The first five lines are balance-sheet figures at 31 March 2027; the rest is the statement of profit and loss for 2026–27.

amt.working: Principal in the twelve EMIs to 31 March 2028

cells.line: Trade payables: micro and small enterprises

amt.working: Security deposits after the two refunds

cells.line: Changes in inventories of finished goods, work in progress and stock in trade

notes.ltb.amt: What stays long-term is only the principal falling due after March 2028.
notes.stb.amt: Schedule III puts current maturities of a long-term loan under short-term borrowings. Principal only: the interest in those EMIs is next year’s cost, not a debt today.
notes.mse.amt: Micro and small only: Mallandur, Sus Gaon, Hinjewadi, Wakad and Bhosari. Paderu’s Udyam certificate says medium and Balewadi has none, so their ₹3,32,000 goes under others.
notes.tcl.amt: The loan’s current portion, every creditor, GST, PF, ESI, professional tax and TDS payable, March salaries and the March power bills: all due within twelve months.
notes.onca.amt: The deposits for the cafés, the roastery and the meters come back only when a lease or a connection ends. Schedule III gives security deposits their own place under other non-current assets.
notes.comc.amt: Green coffee and the raw and packing materials: opening plus purchases less the count. Roasted coffee is finished goods, so it stays out of this line.
notes.chg.amt: More roasted coffee at the end than at the start means less expense, so the change is −₹26,000.
notes.pbt.amt: Before the audit fee and tax, which I add after Kunal’s working.

wrapPartial.text: Your misses below are figures the close would carry wrong, so nothing goes to Meghna until they are fixed. Take them in the order of the close: the bank, the entries, the TB, then the statements.

wrapRetry.text: Start again at the bank: tick every line of the book against the statement, and only the bank’s own entries go into the books. Then ask of each close item whether 2026–27 owns it and whether the TB already has it.

model.intro: The BRS found two entries the bank had made on its own. With them and six more, the suspense went to nil and the TB moved to ₹3,58,51,600 a side. Profit before tax is ₹18,43,320, with the audit fee and tax still to come.

blocks.text: A close starts at the bank, because the bank’s own entries belong in the TB before anything else is mapped. Then each balance gets its proper head. Rounding to ₹ lakh comes last, once every figure ties.

principles: Most BRS differences are timing items, which clear in a few days with no entry, or the bank’s own entries, which the books must take before the trial balance. An error in the book is corrected, never carried.
A close entry follows the period the cost belongs to, not the date on its paper. Check the trial balance first: what is already provided needs no second entry.
Schedule III wants the true head. Principal due within twelve months moves to short-term borrowings, and a medium supplier’s dues go under others, not micro and small.

interview.q: Why do we prepare a bank reconciliation, and what did yours find?
interview.checking: Whether you know which differences wait and which need an entry.
outline: It explains why the bank book and statement differ on a date, and finds what the books missed.
Cheques not yet presented and deposits not yet credited wait; bank charges and direct credits need entries.
In the simulation the BRS turned up ₹1,180 of POS rent and a ₹12,000 refund the books lacked.

interview.q: Your trial balance tallied. Does that mean the books were right?
interview.checking: Whether you know what a tallied trial balance cannot prove.
outline: No. It proves only that debits equal credits; omissions and wrong heads still tally.
In the simulation it tallied with ₹2,24,000 in suspense and no depreciation or March power bill.
So I cleared the suspense, passed the close entries, then split the loan and creditors for Schedule III.
